[2] Consistent with the President's directive in the October 30, 2023 Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence ("AI EO"), [3] the Draft Memo proposes "new agency requirements and guidance for [artificial intelligence ("AI")] governance, innovation, and risk management."[4] In particular, the Draft Memo proposes "minimum practices" for federal agencies when using "rights-impacting [AI]" and "safety-impacting AI,"[5] as well as "a series of recommendations for managing AI risks in the context of Federal procurement."[6]

The Draft Memo appears to attempt to establish a risk-based foundation by only imposing baseline requirements on applications that pose "risks to the rights and safety of the public."[27] However, this approach is undermined by the Draft Memo's definitions and presumptions, which could be read to sweep in lower-risk AI applications.

The Draft Memo currently advises that "[t]o fill potential risk management gaps, agencies are encouraged to promote and to incorporate, as appropriate, additional best practices for AI risk management, such as from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework . . . ."[41] While encouraging agencies to utilize the AI RMF is a good starting point, OMB should go further and encourage federal agency use of the AI RMF by mapping its guidance to the AI RMF, which foregoes a "one-size-fits-all" approach to managing AI risk.

As part of the requirement to complete an AI impact assessment, the Draft Memo prescribes in specific detail the metrics that an agency should use, as well as the content of the impact assessment.[36] Dictating the details of risks assessments threatens to transform these tools from meaningful risk management analyses into rote, check-the-box exercises.

The Draft Memo sets forth three pillars to guide federal agency use of AI-(1) "[s]trengthening AI governance," (2) "[a]dvancing responsible AI innovation," and (3) "[m]anaging risks from the use of AI"[7] -and explicitly states its intent to advance AI innovation within the federal government, making clear that "[a]gencies must increase their capacity to successfully and responsibly adopt AI, including generative AI, into their operations."[8] CTIA broadly agrees with these goals; the federal government must be able to leverage the massive benefits that AI promises, which is critical for AI innovation and leadership on the global scale.

Policymakers considering appropriate responses to AI must ensure that their decisions properly account for the factors that have produced success so far, and that will promote (in the Draft Memo's words) "the scientific, technological, and economic leadership position of the United States in AI."5
